claim: A household of five needs about 45 L a day for drinking and cooking
law: Sphere Handbook basic survival needs: drinking and food 2.5 to 3 L, basic cooking 3 to 6 L per person per day
check: 5 x 9 L = 45 L (upper end of 27.5 to 45 L); the 7.5 L per person emergency minimum for consumption gives 37.5 L

claim: C1 runs on a gravity head of 4.1 to 6.4 kPa (0.42 to 0.66 m), inside the gravity range of STANDARDS 25.6
law: p = rho g h from the raw outlet and fill line (0.95 and 1.19 m) to the clean discharge (0.54 m)
check: 6.44 kPa <= 10 kPa

claim: C1 treats the 45 L day in under 3 hours of filtering even when the module is due for a backflush (2.8 h fouled, 1.5 h clean)
law: Falling-head drain of 3.2 batches of 14.1 L through 0.663 m2 of outside fibre area; assumed clean-water permeability 1,000 L/(m2 h bar), the value used by solutions A and B; fouled at half permeability

claim: Strainer, valve, hoses, fittings and lumens take under a fifth of the mean head, so the membrane sets the flow (18 % at the lowest head; a fouled strainer adds to it)
law: Hagen-Poiseuille for the 9.5 mm hoses and the 0.5 mm lumens (half the leg loss, conservative against a third); K-factor sum 7.7 at the 7 mm barb bore; viscous losses and membrane flux both scale with viscosity, so the share holds in cold water

claim: Flow arithmetic: 1,000 L/(m2 h bar) x 0.66 m2 x 0.05 bar is about 33 L/h gross, 30 L/h net of the other stages
law: L/(m2 h bar) x m2 x bar = L/h
check: claimed 33 L/h, estimate 30.2 L/h (ratio 1.09)

claim: C1 flow of 30 L/h is of the same order as, and conservative against, a new commercial bucket hollow-fibre kit
law: Sawyer PointONE bucket kit: 46.5 to 54 L/h with a 0.3 m hose under a 19 L bucket (CAWST fact sheet)
check: claimed 30.2 L/h, estimate 50 L/h (ratio 0.60)

claim: Flow does not depend on the user: a child or an elderly user gets the same flow, and draws water from the tap in about 9 s per 250 mL cup
law: Gravity drives the filter; tap orifice flow Q = Cd A sqrt(2 g h), Cd 0.6, 8 mm bore, 0.05 to 0.26 m head (1.8 to 4.1 L/min)
check: The persona efforts are pouring a 5 L jug into a rim at 1.27 m (a carer task, not a child's), opening the tap and a gentle syringe push; tap force and pour height to measure in persona trials (HWP-VER-001 TH)

claim: A gentle 30 N push on the 60 mL syringe backflushes the module, inside an elderly user's strength
law: p = F / A on a 26.7 mm bore: 30 N puts at most 54 kPa in the barrel; the luer tip, check valve and barb take much of it, so the stroke is slow and the membrane sees less; 30 N as a light push is assumed
check: Stroke time and membrane pressure to measure; push strength of older users to take from persona trials (TH); a catheter-tip syringe is the alternative if the luer loss is too high

claim: An intact 0.1 um hollow-fibre membrane is a size barrier for bacteria (about 0.3 to 5 um) and protozoan cysts (about 3 to 15 um); no removal is claimed from the pore label
law: Size exclusion: Cryptosporidium oocysts 4 to 6 um and Giardia cysts 8 to 12 um are 40 to 120 times the pore; a commercial 0.1 um bucket module tested above 7 log Klebsiella and 5 log Cryptosporidium and Giardia (CAWST fact sheet)
check: A log reduction exists for this module only once an accredited laboratory measures it (HWP-VER-001 TA, TB)

claim: The membrane is not a virus barrier, so C carries the no-virus warning and pairs with chlorine in the raw bucket (solution D) where viruses are a risk
law: Enteric viruses about 0.02 to 0.1 um pass a 0.1 um pore; the cited 0.1 um bucket module lists viruses as not removed (CAWST)
check: No virus claim (Amish, 2026-11-11: no virus claim, co-treat); HWP-CLM-001 warning on the raw bucket label

claim: Paired with D, 30 minutes at a measured free chlorine residual of 0.5 mg/L at the end of contact gives a CT of 15 mg min/L, above the 4 log virus CT even at 0.5 degC (12); mixing and the residual are D's to confirm
law: CT = C x t with C the residual at the end of contact; EPA free chlorine CT for 4 log virus inactivation, pH 6 to 9: 12 at 0.5 degC, 8 at 5 degC, 3 at 20 degC mg min/L
check: 15 mg min/L >= 12 mg min/L

claim: Chlorine does not inactivate Cryptosporidium at household doses (136 h at 1.875 mg/L for a CT of 15,300, longer in cold water), nor reach a useful Giardia CT in 30 minutes, so the membrane after chlorination is what removes cysts
law: CT for Cryptosporidium with free chlorine about 15,300 mg min/L at about 25 degC (CDC hyperchlorination guidance); HWP-CLM-001: no Cryptosporidium claim from chlorine alone
check: Chlorinate first, then filter: the order of the C plus D system; each barrier covers the other's gap

claim: The PVDF fibres tolerate a lifetime of household chlorine in the raw water (98,550 ppm h over 3 years at 3.75 mg/L, continuously wetted)
law: Lifetime chlorine tolerance of a PVDF UF membrane 3,000,000 ppm h (LG Water Solutions data, another maker's product); hydrophilising additives, potting and gaskets may tolerate less
check: 3.3 % of limit <= 100 % of limit

claim: Free chlorine passes the membrane, so a residual reaches the clean bucket and protects stored water; C has no carbon stage, because carbon downstream of the dose would remove that residual
law: Hypochlorous acid and hypochlorite are small dissolved species that a 0.1 um membrane does not retain; activated carbon reduces free chlorine fast (the basis of NSF/ANSI 42 chlorine claims); CDC SWS target above 0.2 mg/L after 24 h
check: Residual in the clean bucket to measure at 1 and 24 h with D (HWP-VER-001 TJ); chlorine taste is the trade-off (HWC-DEC-001 D3)

claim: Settling for 1 h (1.5 h below 10 degC) drops silt of 10 um and larger below the outlet: 0.74 h needed at 20 degC and 1.13 h at 5 degC for the 241 mm column
law: Stokes settling v = g d2 (rho_p - rho) / 18 mu, quartz 2,650 kg/m3, mu 1.0 (20 degC) and 1.52 mPa s (5 degC); clay (2 um, 13 mm/h) and colloids do not settle; pouring and draw-off can resuspend fines
check: 1.13 h at 5 degC <= 1.5 h at 5 degC

claim: Cotton cloth folded to eight layers in the fill ring removes coarse particles and plankton-attached organisms before the bucket
law: Colwell et al. 2003 (PNAS): worn, laundered sari cloth folded four to eight times has an effective pore of about 20 um; 48 % fewer cholera cases in 65 villages
check: A prefilter only; no pathogen claim rests on it; the cloth is specified as worn, soft and tightly woven, and its retention is measured at TRL 4 (TD)

claim: Turbid source water (SC3, 10 to 100 NTU) needs more backflushes, not a different design
law: Commercial 0.1 um bucket kit: backflush about every 3,800 L of clear water and every 40 L or less of very turbid water (CAWST)
check: Volume between backflushes at 1, 10, 50 and 100 NTU to measure (HWP-VER-001 TE); settle overnight above 50 NTU

claim: The loaded stand needs 18.7 deg of tilt and 78 N at 1 m to tip (the briefed 420 mm frame gave 14.2 deg and failed); a child's pull can exceed 78 N, so a wall strap is fitted (HWC-DEC-001 D4)
law: Tip angle atan(half base / centre of gravity height), raw bucket full, clean bucket empty; criterion 15 deg (assumed, as solution B)
check: 18.7 deg >= 15 deg

claim: The module runs full: shell air would block fibre area, so the module stands upright with its raw inlet on top and a bleed screw at the top of the shell, opened at first fill until water shows
law: A wetted membrane holds air below its bubble point (hundreds of kPa for real 0.1 um fibres), so trapped shell air cannot pass the fibres; downflow in the hose (about 0.12 m/s) roughly cancels bubble rise, so venting through the inlet alone is not reliable
check: Failed as briefed (orientation free; air pockets over the U-bends), fixed by the upright mounting and a bleed screw on the top cap (supplier request); repeat the bleed after a dry spell

claim: Even a raw bucket filled to the brim (19.4 L above the settling zone) fits in the clean bucket when the user starts below the 2.5 L refill line
law: Volume balance; as briefed, two 20 L containers overflow when the clean one is not empty, and a 5 L line still overflowed if the user overfilled past the 17 L mark; fixed with a 2.5 L refill line just above the tap
check: in 19.56 L, out 19.4 L

claim: Chlorine is added after settling, through the lid port, and the raw valve stays shut for 30 minutes
law: Turbidity shields organisms and adds chlorine demand (WHO, CDC: double dose for turbid water); an open valve during contact sends water to the filter before its 30 minutes
check: Failed as briefed (no hold point), fixed: a dosing port in the raw lid for D and a valve tag 'shut for 30 minutes after dosing'; mixing and dose belong to D

claim: An air hold test shows a broken fibre as bubbles in the clear raw hose: the user pumps air strokes through a luer check valve until a firm 56 N push (100 kPa) holds
law: Young-Laplace dP = 4 gamma / d: at 100 kPa any opening above about 3 um passes air, while real 0.1 um fibres hold air to hundreds of kPa; the lumens hold 52 mL of water, which the first strokes push out through the walls; Boyle's law then needs several strokes, which the check valve allows; the push force is the user's gauge
check: Failed as first written (one 60 mL stroke cannot reach 100 kPa against a water-filled clean side), fixed with the check valve and a several-stroke procedure

claim: The air test finds gross damage, not small defects, so it is a monthly check and never proof of performance
law: Openings under about 3 um hold at 100 kPa; bacteria are 0.5 to 5 um; a broken fibre (0.5 mm lumen) passes air at 0.6 kPa
check: Instructions say 'retire if bubbles stream', never 'safe if no bubbles'; the module maker's production integrity test (HWP-VER-001 TI) is the real proof

claim: The clean side is above atmospheric pressure (1.7 kPa at the module outlet) while filtering, so a leaking clean fitting drips out and cannot draw dirty water in
law: Hydrostatic pressure from the clean discharge (0.54 m) down to the module outlet (0.36 m); every clean-side joint outside the module sits below the discharge except the inlet barb at it
check: 1.72 kPa >= 0 kPa

claim: Wet fibres can be damaged by freezing without any change in flow, so C carries a do-not-freeze warning and a retire-after-freezing rule
law: Water expands about 9 % on freezing; a silent failure mode that hollow-fibre makers warn of (concept validation questions, item 17)
check: No freeze claim; pictogram; after a suspected freeze the module is retired, not tested and reused; drain and store indoors (HWP-VER-001 TF)

claim: The module shell, end caps and potting hold the highest raw pressure (8.2 kPa) and a hard backflush (179 kPa)
law: Thin-wall hoop stress p r / t on a 50 x 2 mm shell is 2.1 MPa at 179 kPa, far below 10 MPa (assumed for PP or ABS); the end load (about 300 N) on caps and potting is not checked; a palm push of 200 N doubles the pressure
check: Supplier's burst and backwash rating to obtain (HWC-DEC-001 C2); the instruction is a gentle push

claim: A gentle backflush (54 kPa) stays inside the module maker's backwash limit
law: p = F / syringe bore area; the maximum backwash pressure of the bought module is not yet known
check: To confirm from the supplier (HWC-DEC-001 C2); the instruction is a gentle push with water drawn from the clean tap

claim: Without chlorine, water standing on the clean side (83 mL: 52 mL in the lumens, the rest in the tee and clean hose) and in the clean bucket can regrow bacteria between batches
law: Biofilm grows on wetted surfaces downstream of membranes (Rev A specification section 05); stored water is recontaminated in handling (HWP-SRC-001 SC5)
check: Mitigations: closed bucket with tap and screened vent, no dipping, weekly chlorine rinse of the clean bucket, discard the first cup after a pause of more than a day, D residual where used; regrowth to measure (HWP-VER-001 TE, TG)

claim: Every wetted material is from a family available in NSF/ANSI/CAN 61 grades: HDPE buckets, PP valve, tap and fittings, silicone hose, EPDM gaskets, 316 stainless strainer, PVDF fibres, polyurethane or epoxy potting
law: NSF/ANSI/CAN 61 and 372; buckets must be new food-grade, never reused chemical pails; plasticised PVC hose is avoided because plasticisers can leach
check: Extractables of the actual grades and the potting (HWP-VER-001 TG); prototypes are used with known potable test water only

claim: Full, the C1 system weighs about 50 kg (raw 17 L and clean 20 L of water, buckets, stand, module)
law: Two buckets of water (17 + 20 kg), buckets 2.4 kg, stand 9 kg (timber 500 kg/m3), module and hoses 1 kg
check: claimed 50 kg, estimate 49.4 kg (ratio 1.01)

claim: C2: four ceramic candles under about 0.3 m of water give about 4 L/h full, so the 45 L day takes about 19 h of filtering
law: British Berkefeld gravity data: two candles 2 L/h in the 12 L system (about 1 L/h per candle); flow falls as the upper chamber drains (mean 60 %, assumed)
check: Physics holds; 19 h is a best case for new candles; the option filters most of the day and night and misses the 'few hours' target (scored in HWC-OPT-001)

claim: C2: silver-impregnated ceramic candles reduce bacteria (4 log listed) and protozoa by size exclusion; any silver claim needs biocide registration and silver leaching data
law: Engineering for Change listing (4 log bacteria; virus and cyst data unknown); WHO gives no health-based silver value and notes up to 0.1 mg/L is tolerated; HWP-REG-001 W9
check: No silver or antimicrobial claim; plain ceramic is an option; silver in water to measure (TG)

claim: C2: ceramic is brittle and cracks from a drop or from freezing without any visible change in flow
law: Fired ceramic has low fracture toughness; a hairline crack opens a path far larger than the pores
check: Inspect candles at each cleaning; retire after a drop; no freeze claim

claim: C3: a plastic biosand filter treats 18 L batches at up to 0.4 L/min and needs a pause of at least 1 h between batches, so the 45 L day takes 2.5 batches
law: CAWST 2009 fact sheet: maximum 0.4 L/min, loading rate below 600 L/(h m2) (199 here), 12 to 18 L per batch, pause 1 to 48 h
check: Physics holds; the day's water is filtered in three sessions spread through the day

claim: C3: biosand reduces bacteria less than a membrane (up to 96.5 % in the lab, 87.9 to 98.5 % in the field, about 1 to 1.8 log) and protozoa more than 99.9 % in the lab, after a biolayer ripens for up to 30 days
law: CAWST 2009 fact sheet; removal is low and silent while the biolayer ripens and after disturbance
check: Holds as a principle; below the WHO two-star 2 log bacteria target in all cited data; chlorine must go after the filter, never before it, or it harms the biolayer

claim: C3: the filter holds about 124 kg of dry sand and gravel (about 170 kg in operation with pore and standing water), so it is filled in place and never moved
law: Bed volume (392 mm bore, 0.64 m of media) x 1,600 kg/m3 bulk density (assumed)
check: claimed 124 kg, estimate 124 kg (ratio 1.00)
